passages.text: Association Between Glucocerebrosidase Mutations and Parkinson's Disease in Ireland

Multiple studies implicate heterozygous <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> mutations as a major genetic risk factor for Parkinson's disease (PD); however, the frequency of mutations has never been examined in PD patients from the Irish population. <sentence_start/>We prospectively recruited 314 unrelated Irish PD patients (UK Brain Bank Criteria) and 96 Irish healthy controls (without any signs or family history of parkinsonism) attending. <sentence_start/>The Dublin Neurological Institute (DNI). <sentence_start/>Complete exon <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> Sanger sequencing analysis with flanking intronic regions was performed. <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> carrier frequency was 8.3% in PD and 3.1% in controls. <sentence_start/>We identified a number of potentially pathogenic mutations including a p.G195E substitution and a p.G377C variant, previously described in a case study of Gaucher's disease in Ireland. <sentence_start/>On genotype-phenotype assessment hallucinations, dyskinesia, and dystonia were more prevalent in <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic>-PD. <sentence_start/>The genetic etiology of PD in Ireland differs from the continental Europe as seen with the lower <italic toggle="yes">LRRK2</italic> and higher than in most European countries <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> mutation frequency. <sentence_start/>Determining genetic risk factors in different ethnicities will be critical for future personalized therapeutic approach.
Introduction

Glucocerebrosidase gene (<italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic>) encodes <italic toggle="yes">B</italic>-glucocerebrosidase enzyme hydrolyzing glucocerebroside to glucose and ceramide. <sentence_start/>While homozygous or compound heterozygous <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> mutations alter glucocerebrosidase activity and result in a recessive lysosomal-storage disorder, Gaucher's disease, heterozygous variants have been implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD) pathogenesis (<citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1474-4422(12)70190-4" pmid="23079555" pmcid="PMC4141416" count="1">1</citation>-<citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.mcn.2015.03.013" pmid="25802027" pmcid="PMC4471139" count="1">3</citation>). <sentence_start/>In fact, <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> mutations have been identified as one of the strongest known genetic risk factors for PD (5-20% of PD patients are reported to harbor <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> mutations depending on ethnicity) (<citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3233/JPD-171092" pmid="28598856" count="1">2</citation>). <sentence_start/>Initially, <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic>-related PD was thought to reflect the clinical phenotype of idiopathic PD (<citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.mcn.2015.03.013" pmid="25802027" pmcid="PMC4471139" count="1">3</citation>); however, current evidence suggests unique motor (e.g., frequent falls, freezing of gait, dyskinesia, faster progression), non-motor [autonomic symptoms, younger age at onset (2.6-0.9 year earlier age at onset)] (<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.27659" pmid="30957308" pmcid="PMC6579628" count="1">4</citation>), increased prevalence of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) and daytime sleepiness (<citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/NXG.0000000000000354" pmid="31404238" pmcid="PMC6659137" count="1">5</citation>) features and cognitive impairment (frequent cognitive decline and hallucinations) (<citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/NXG.0000000000000354" pmid="31404238" pmcid="PMC6659137" count="1">5</citation>-<citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamaneurol.2014.2950" pmid="25506732" pmcid="PMC4326672" count="1">7</citation>).

The <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> gene is located on chromosome 1q22 and consists of 11 coding exons. <sentence_start/>The existence of a highly homologous pseudogene (GBAP1) (sharing 96% of exonic sequence) located 16 kb downstream of the functional <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> gene makes <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> sequencing studies challenging (<citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/0888-7543(89)90319-4" pmid="2914709" count="1">8</citation>). <sentence_start/>Sequencing of all exons and using long-range PCR primers specific for the functional <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> gene is the most reliable method for genetic screening. <sentence_start/>However, many centers continue to restrict the analysis to the most common variants or exons where most of the mutations are reported (exons 9 and 10) (<citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddq454" pmid="20947659" count="1">9</citation>). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> p.L444P and p.N370S are the two most common pathogenic substitutions among 335 reported, responsible for 50-70% of cases (<citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1474-4422(12)70190-4" pmid="23079555" pmcid="PMC4141416" count="1">1</citation>). <sentence_start/>Based on homozygous and compound heterozygous mutations resulting in specific subtypes of Gaucher's disease, <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> mutations can be classified as “mild” (p.N370S and p.R496H) and “severe” [p.L444P, p.D380A, p.R131C, p.D409H, p.R463C, p.R257Q, p.V394L, c.1263-1317del, and RecNciI-a recombinant allele (p.L444P-A456P-V460V)] (<citation rid="B10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000001315" pmid="25653295" pmcid="PMC4351661" count="1">10</citation>). <sentence_start/>Carriers of mild mutations are reported to have 2.2-fold higher risk of PD and mean age at onset of 58.1 (±10.6), while carriers of severe mutations have 9.92- to 21.29-fold increased risk of PD and mean age at onset of 52.1 (±11.2) (<citation rid="B10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000001315" pmid="25653295" pmcid="PMC4351661" count="1">10</citation>, <citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/brain/awz350" pmid="31755958" pmcid="PMC6935749" count="1">11</citation>). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> p.E326K homozygous and compound heterozygous mutations do not cause Gaucher's disease; thus, there may be a distinct mechanism predisposing to PD in carriers of p.E326K. Until recently, believed to be a benign polymorphism, now p.E326K is an established risk factor (large meta-analyses) causing rapid motor progression of PD (β = 3.42; 95% CI, 0.66-6.17; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.02) (<citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.3043" pmid="25064009" pmcid="PMC4146673" count="1">12</citation>, <citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamaneurol.2016.2245" pmid="27571329" pmcid="PMC5056861" count="1">13</citation>), cognitive decline, and the development of RBD among those who did not have the disorder at baseline (<citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/NXG.0000000000000354" pmid="31404238" pmcid="PMC6659137" count="1">5</citation>, <citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.27845" pmid="31505070" pmcid="PMC7017876" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/brain/awz350" pmid="31755958" pmcid="PMC6935749" count="1">11</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similarly, there is an emerging trend in the literature to classify p.T369M as a risk variant (with the reported effect size similar to that of p.E326K, baseline RBD, associated cognitive decline, and higher hazard ratio of reaching H&Y3) (<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.27659" pmid="30957308" pmcid="PMC6579628" count="1">4</citation>, <citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.27845" pmid="31505070" pmcid="PMC7017876" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.27803" pmid="31769092" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/NXG.0000000000000104" pmid="27648471" pmcid="PMC5017539" count="1">15</citation>).

The prevalence of <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> mutations can vary according to ethnicity (<citation rid="B10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000001315" pmid="25653295" pmcid="PMC4351661" count="1">10</citation>) (e.g., mutations are common in Ashkenazi Jewish populations). <sentence_start/>Locally derived data are important for further genetic characterization, development of local guidelines, enrolment in clinical trials, and search for the disease-modifying treatments. <sentence_start/>Large Irish families, small population size of the country (Republic of Ireland population, 4.79 million in 2017, as per the most recent census) (<citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" count="1">16</citation>), and relative isolation from the continental Europe make the Irish population ideal for genetic studies. <sentence_start/>We and others reported that genetics of PD in the Irish population differs from that in the continental Europe, e.g., <italic toggle="yes">LRRK2</italic> mutations are rare (<citation rid="B17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.parkreldis.2005.05.004" pmid="16102999" count="1">17</citation>). <sentence_start/>We have shown in a recent epidemiological study that the population structure in Ireland differs from the rest of the Europe, and this may be related to the Celtic ancestry (<citation rid="B18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pgen.1007152" pmid="29370172" pmcid="PMC5784891" count="1">18</citation>). <sentence_start/>We have also demonstrated that the prevalence of another neurological condition, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) in Ireland, differs from other European countries (<citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/jmedgenet-2013-101795" pmid="23881933" pmcid="PMC3812897" count="1">19</citation>). <sentence_start/>The prevalence of <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> in PD and genotype-phenotype correlation has never been studied in Ireland, and we hypothesized that similarly to <italic toggle="yes">LRRK2</italic>, it may differ from that in other populations.
Methods
Ethical Approval
The ethical approval (1/378/1,300) was granted by the Mater Misericordiae University Hospital (MMUH), Dublin, Ireland. <sentence_start/>Informed written consent was obtained.
Design
This is an observational cross-sectional study.
Participants

Three hundred fourteen unrelated Irish patients over age 18 diagnosed with PD (UK Brain Bank Criteria) were recruited from a tertiary referral center, Dublin Neurological Institute (DNI), at the MMUH, Dublin, Ireland. <sentence_start/>Patient's attending the DNI reside in the Dublin city or rural areas of the country. <sentence_start/>To expand the diversity of participants, an additional notice about the study recruitment was posted on the Irish Parkinson's Association website. <sentence_start/>Secondary and atypical forms of parkinsonism were excluded. <sentence_start/>Ninety-six healthy controls (friends or spouses of patients) without any signs or family history of parkinsonism, over age 18 were recruited from the DNI.
Sequencing and Data Analysis

Genomic DNA was isolated from peripheral blood lymphocytes using QIAmp Blood Midi Kit. <sentence_start/>Genetic analysis was performed at the Department of Neuroscience, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, FL, USA. <sentence_start/>All PD patients were prescreened for the most common genetic causes of autosomal dominant disease (<italic toggle="yes">LRRK2, SNCA, VPS35</italic>) and patients with young onset PD (YOPD) (age, <50) also for autosomal recessive PD (<italic toggle="yes">PARKIN, PINK1, DJ1</italic>). <sentence_start/>PD patients (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 314) were tested for specific point mutations; LRRK2 p.G2019S, SNCA p. A53T, and p.A30P and VPS35 p.D620N (TaqMan Allelic Discrimination Assay, on Quant Studio System Real-Time PCR System). <sentence_start/>Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) analysis was employed to determine the dosage alterations in <italic toggle="yes">SNCA</italic>. <sentence_start/>PD patients with YOPD (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 81) were investigated by Sanger sequencing of all coding exons plus 25 base pairs of exon-intron boundary of <italic toggle="yes">PARKIN</italic> (12 exons), <italic toggle="yes">PINK1</italic> (8 exons), and <italic toggle="yes">DJ1</italic> (6 exons) genes. <sentence_start/>MLPA analysis was also performed.

<italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> sequencing of all 11 coding exons plus 25 base pairs of exon-intron boundary was performed on all patients and 96 controls and confirmed bidirectionally. <sentence_start/>PCR and primer sequences are available in Supplementary Tables 1, 2. <sentence_start/>The pathogenicity of the variants was determined based on the current literature and <italic toggle="yes">in silico</italic> tools [Polyphen v2 (<citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nmeth0410-248" pmid="20354512" pmcid="PMC2855889" count="1">20</citation>), SIFT (<citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nprot.2009.86" pmid="19561590" count="1">21</citation>), Mutation Taster (<citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nmeth.2890" pmid="24681721" count="1">22</citation>)] (Table 1). <sentence_start/>Results are presented in Table 2. <sentence_start/>Both newer and well-established historical nomenclature (GBA protein −39 amino acids) for <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> variants annotation was used.

Samples from two patients were tested for β-glucosidase enzyme level and chitoriosidase level by the use of a validated functional assay (fluorimetric assay method) (<citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00216-011-5496-z" pmid="22033823" pmcid="PMC3351006" count="1">23</citation>) at the Guy's Hospital, London, United Kingdom.
Statistical Analysis

Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics, Version 22.0. <sentence_start/>Cohort characteristics were assessed using descriptive statistics. <sentence_start/>Bivariate associations between categorical variables were calculated using Pearson chi-square tests (<italic toggle="yes">X</italic><sup>2</sup>) or Fisher's exact tests (when expected cell counts ≤ 5 observations, e.g., genotype frequencies comparison). <sentence_start/>Where continuous variables were normally distributed, independent sample <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>-tests were used, and where not, Mann-Whitney <italic toggle="yes">U</italic>-tests. <sentence_start/>The results were deemed statistically significant where <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.05. <sentence_start/>Two hypotheses were tested. <sentence_start/>The first was that the presence of a <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> variant increased the risk of PD in the Irish population. <sentence_start/>Logistic regression model was used to control for age and gender. <sentence_start/>The second hypothesis was that the <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> variant carriers have earlier age-at-PD onset (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.27803" pmid="31769092" count="1">14</citation>). <sentence_start/>A linear regression model was fitted with age at onset as the dependent variable and the presence or absence of a <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> variant as the independent variable (gender as a covariate). <sentence_start/>Linear and logistic regression models were used to test whether the frequency of the motor complications, wearing off, dyskinesia, dystonia, freezing of gait, hallucinations, dementia, and Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Score part III (UPDRS-III) differed between carriers and non-carriers. <sentence_start/>Gender, age, and disease duration were considered as covariates. <sentence_start/>In the sensitivity analysis, each of the motor complications was also controlled for medications, UPDRS-III score, and disease subtype.
Results

We screened 314 Irish patients with PD of which 62.4% (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 196) were male and 37.6% (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 118) were female, with mean age at inclusion of 64.94 ± 10.69 years, mean age at onset of 56.23 ± 12.04 years, and mean disease duration of 8.62 ± 6.97 years. <sentence_start/>The majority had tremor-predominant disease (55.7%), followed by postural instability gait disorder (PIGD) (34.1%) and mixed subtypes (10.2%). <sentence_start/>Motor complications were seen in 43.3%. <sentence_start/>Family history of PD was present in 173 patients (55.1%). <sentence_start/>A group of 96 Irish controls [51% men (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 49), 49% women (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 47), mean age at inclusion (61.15 ± 14.5)] was studied to assess the mutation frequency in the ethnically matched population.

We examined 314 patients for genes associated with autosomal dominant PD. <sentence_start/>Among 314 patients, we identified one PD patient with LRRK2 G2019S mutation positive for <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> benign intronic variant (exon 7−18 bp). <sentence_start/>We did not identify any carriers of p.A53T or p.A30P in SNCA or p.D620N in VPS35. <sentence_start/>There were no patients with <italic toggle="yes">SNCA</italic> dosage alterations.

On examination of the 81 patients with YOPD, we identified one homozygote carrier (p.G430D/p.G430D), three compound heterozygote (p.Leu112fsX163/p.R275W; p.G430D/Ex 4&5del; p.R275W/Ex3 del), and three heterozygote carriers [p.R275W/wt. <sentence_start/>(<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 1); p.P437L/wt (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 2)] in <italic toggle="yes">PARKIN</italic> gene. <sentence_start/>None of the <italic toggle="yes">PARKIN</italic> gene carriers had variants in <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> detected. <sentence_start/>No homozygous or compound heterozygous carriers of <italic toggle="yes">PINK1</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">DJ1</italic> were detected.

We detected 26 carriers of <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> pathogenic/risk variants in PD and 3 in controls [p.E326K, P.T369M, p.N370S, p.F216Y, p.D409H, and RecNcil (p.L444P-A456P-V460V)] (Tables 2, 3). <sentence_start/>These variants were found in 8.3% of PD patients and 3.1% of controls (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.08, <italic toggle="yes">X</italic><sup>2</sup>). <sentence_start/>The result remained non-significant after controlling for age and gender [odd's ratio (OR), 3.2 (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.06; 95%CI, 0.94-10.97). <sentence_start/>RecNcil and p.N370S carrier frequency in PD was 1.9% [RecNcil, <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3, minor allele frequency (MAF) = 0.48%; p.N370S, <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3, MAF = 0.478%); these variants represented 18.2% (6/33) of the pathogenic/risk variants and were not present in controls. <sentence_start/>The frequency of <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> mutations in familial PD was 8.1% (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 14) and 8.6% (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 12) in sporadic PD. <sentence_start/>The most common variants detected in PD were the risk variants: p.E326K (12 heterozygotes including p.E326K/G377C and p.E326K/T369M and 1 homozygote, p.E326K/E326K) and p.T369M (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 6, including mentioned above p.E326K/T369M), followed by the pathogenic variants: RecNcil (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3) and p.N370S (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3) (Tables 2-4). <sentence_start/>Additionally, we detected three variants of unknown significance (VUS), p.G195E, p.R301H, and p.R368C, in three PD patients and none in controls (Tables 1, 4). <sentence_start/>We also identified 11 carriers of benign, known intronic variants (rs140335079, T > A: three heterozygotes, five homozygotes; exon 7-17 bp, G > C: one homozygote; rs377143075, T > C: two heterozygotes).

The mean age at onset for the mild mutation carriers (p.N370S <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3) was 66 (±4.58) years, while for the severe mutations (p.D409H, <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 1; RecNcil, <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 3), it was 50 (±13.56) years (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.11, independent <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>-test). <sentence_start/>The mean age at onset for the risk variants carriers (p.E326K, <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 12; p.T369M, <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 6 including p.E326K/p.T369M) was 54.66 (±11.15).

We found a VUS p.R301H variant, which has not been previously reported either in ExAC (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature19057" pmid="27535533" pmcid="PMC5018207" count="1">24</citation>) or gnomAD (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature19057" pmid="27535533" pmcid="PMC5018207" count="1">24</citation>) databases in a homozygous state. <sentence_start/>The affected was a man with PIGD from age 57 years, normal cognition, and Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) stage 3 who was asymptomatic for Gaucher's disease. <sentence_start/>We detected two very interesting variants. <sentence_start/>p.G195E reported in Gaucher's disease, but not in PD, predicted to be pathogenic by <italic toggle="yes">in silico</italic> tools (<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1172/JCI119437" pmid="9153297" pmcid="PMC508094" count="1">25</citation>) in a 69-year-old man. <sentence_start/>β-Glucosidase enzyme level was measured, and it was at 10.3 nmol/h/mg protein (normal range, 8.4-32.8), and plasma chitoriosidase level was normal. <sentence_start/>The patient had unilateral, tremor-predominant, levodopa-responsive PD and normal cognition from age 54 years (Figure 13-1). <sentence_start/>Later on, his cognition declined (MoCA score was 25/30: visuospatial/executive abilities and delayed recall were affected), but hallucinations were not present. <sentence_start/>He had mild drooling of saliva during the nighttime and REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD). <sentence_start/>His medications included carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 mg four times daily, mirabegron 50 mg for urinary frequency, and citalopram 15 mg for well-controlled depression. <sentence_start/>He was also on a continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) machine for an obstructive sleep apnea. <sentence_start/>His MRI brain was normal, and dopamine transporter single photon emission computerized tomography (DaT scan) showed a decreased dopamine tracer uptake more pronounced on the left side of the brain. <sentence_start/>On examination he was hypophonic, had slight rigidity in all limbs, and was bradykinetic more on the right than on the left side. <sentence_start/>He had bilateral postural and kinetic hand tremor without rest tremor. <sentence_start/>He did not have any other motor complications.
Figure 1

Family pedigree of the patient with <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> p.G195E variant in exon 6, rs74462743: red, affected with Parkinson's disease (PD); blue, tested and positive for p.G195E variant; green, tested and negative for p.G195E variant; arrow, proband; diagonal line, deceased.

There was a PD history in his maternal aunt (deceased) (Figure 12-13), maternal uncle (deceased) (Figure 12-10) and in his 67-year-old cousin (deceased) (Figure 13-8). <sentence_start/>He had tremor-predominant PD since age 51 years and was positive for the same variant. <sentence_start/>Initially, he was started on mirapexin for 2 years. <sentence_start/>He developed hallucinations at age 56 (benign, mainly animals) treated with quetiapine 25 mg in the morning and 50 mg at night. <sentence_start/>He became forgetful, developed dementia (MoCA score, 7/30), and was commenced on donepezil 10 mg once a day and memantine 10 mg twice a day. <sentence_start/>He then was switched to carbidopa/levodopa preparation 25/100 mg two tablets three times daily. <sentence_start/>His other non-motor symptoms included depression-stable on venlafaxine (effexor XL) 150 and 75 mg, and RBD. <sentence_start/>He was unable to turn in bed and get out of a chair without help and had freezing of gait episodes. <sentence_start/>There was no wearing off or dyskinesia present. <sentence_start/>He needed assistance with cutting food, dressing up, and hygiene. <sentence_start/>His swallow became affected with occasional choking episodes; therefore, he was commenced on thickened fluid diet. <sentence_start/>He had a urinary catheter <italic toggle="yes">in situ</italic> due to the difficulties arising from the urinary urgency. <sentence_start/>The biggest problem was agitation in the evening. <sentence_start/>At the time of recruitment, he was wheelchair bound, and his UPDRS-III score was 28. <sentence_start/>On examination, there was slight, however ongoing, resting tremor and bilateral, severe bradykinesia, and rigidity. <sentence_start/>The dopamine uptake on the DaT scan at age 65 was reported as profoundly decreased. <sentence_start/>The variant was absent in two asymptomatic siblings of the proband age 57 and 67 (Table 3). <sentence_start/>Neurological examination was normal in both cases, and MoCA test was 30/30 in the sister (<bold>Figure 1</bold>3-7) and 29/30 in the brother (Figure 13-5). <sentence_start/>There were no subtle signs of Gaucher's disease with normal hematology, biochemistry, and liver tests.

The second interesting variant found was p.G377C (c.1246 G > T) variant (not reported in databases), predicted to be pathogenic by <italic toggle="yes">in silico</italic> tools (Tables 1, 2) in a 54-year-old man (Figure 23-1). <sentence_start/>On further analysis, the β-glucosidase enzyme level was 10.8 nmol/h/mg protein (normal range, 8.4-32.8). <sentence_start/>The enzyme level in simultaneous controls was 13.6, 14.2, and 14.4. <sentence_start/>The level of plasma chitotriosidase was normal (as expected in a heterozygous asymptomatic for Gaucher's disease patient). <sentence_start/>The patient had tremor-predominant PD and normal cognition since age 39 years. <sentence_start/>There were no hallucinations. <sentence_start/>At 42 years old, he developed dyskinesia, which was treated by a deep brain stimulator (DBS) at age 49. <sentence_start/>He also had dystonia and micrographia (the majority of the words was not legible when written). <sentence_start/>At the time of recruitment, he was on amantadine 100 mg twice a day, selegiline 5 mg, slow release levodopa preparation at night (half-sinemet CR), and carbidopa/levodopa 50/12.5 mg five times a day. <sentence_start/>On examination, there was hypophonia, moderately stooped posture, and slow gait. <sentence_start/>PD was present in his mother diagnosed at age 45 (Figure 22-6), who died at 73, maternal aunt diagnosed in her 70s (deceased at 78) (Figure 22-9), and maternal grandfather (Figure 21-3).
Figure 2

Family pedigree of the patient with <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> p.E326K variant in exon 8 and p.G377C variant in exon 9: red, affected with Parkinson's disease (PD); blue, tested and positive for p.E326K/G377C variant; arrow, proband; diagonal line, deceased.

On genotype-phenotype assessment between 26 mutation/risk variant carriers and 285 non-carriers, the median age at onset in both groups was the same (57 years), carriers were more likely to be a female (53.8% carrier women vs. 46.2% carrier men, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.08, <italic toggle="yes">X</italic><sup>2</sup>), and the majority (65.4%) of carriers had late onset PD (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 17, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.31, <italic toggle="yes">X</italic><sup>2</sup>) and reported having a positive PD family history (53.8%, <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 14, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.87, <italic toggle="yes">X</italic><sup>2</sup>) (Table 5). <sentence_start/>However, these results were statistically non-significant (Table 1). <sentence_start/>Cognitive problems were present in 34.6% of carriers in comparison to 29.8% in non-carriers; however, the <italic toggle="yes">p</italic>-value was non-significant. <sentence_start/>Hallucinations were four times more prevalent in carriers than non-carriers [<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.01, OR 3.97 (95%CI 1.434-11.015), Fisher's exact test]. <sentence_start/>This remained true after adjusting for age, gender, disease duration, dementia, cognitive impairment, and medications. <sentence_start/>While additionally controlled for the presence of <italic toggle="yes">Parkin</italic> homozygous/compound heterozygous or <italic toggle="yes">LRRK2</italic> mutations, the prevalence of hallucinations in <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> mutation carriers remained significantly higher than in <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> non-carriers [<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.04, OR 4 (95%CI 1.1-15.3)]. <sentence_start/>In terms of motor complications dyskinesia [<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.003, OR 3.36 (95%CI 1.46-7.75, <italic toggle="yes">X</italic><sup>2</sup> test)] and dystonia [<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.009, OR 12.261 (95% CI 2.34-64.212, Fisher's exact test)] were more prevalent in carriers vs. non-carriers and were independently associated with the carrier status after controlling for age, gender, disease duration, medications, UPDRS III score, and subtypes. <sentence_start/>When the presence of dyskinesia and dystonia was controlled for the presence of <italic toggle="yes">PARKIN</italic> homozygous/compound heterozygous or <italic toggle="yes">LRRK2</italic> mutations, the result for dyskinesia remained significant [dyskinesia: <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.007, OR 4.37 (95%CI 1.49-12.85)], but it became non-significant for dystonia (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.088). <sentence_start/>There was no association found between other variables and <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> status (Table 5).
Discussion

<italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> mutations carried in the heterozygous state are a strong risk factor for developing α-synucleinopathy including PD. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> variants also appear to act as phenotypic modifiers affecting cognition and motor progression of PD. <sentence_start/>The frequency of <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> variants differs across populations (<citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddq454" pmid="20947659" count="1">9</citation>, <citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/brain/awv179" pmid="26117366" pmcid="PMC4564023" count="1">26</citation>, <citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/01.wnl.0000304039.11891.29" pmid="18434642" count="1">27</citation>), and herein, we show that patients with PD in Ireland have a relatively high frequency of <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> mutations (PD, 8.3%; controls, 3.1%). <sentence_start/>The frequency is higher than that of the Portuguese (6.1%, 14/230) (<citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neurobiolaging.2007.11.016" pmid="18160183" pmcid="PMC2736795" count="1">28</citation>), Greek (4.7%, 8/172) (<citation rid="B29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neulet.2009.01.029" pmid="19383421" count="1">29</citation>), Flanders-Belgian population (4.5%, 12/266) (<citation rid="B30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neulet.2016.07.008" pmid="27397011" count="1">30</citation>), and British (4.2%, 33/790) (<citation rid="B10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/WNL.0000000000001315" pmid="25653295" pmcid="PMC4351661" count="1">10</citation>), and slightly above the average European carrier frequency (6.7%, 76/1,130) (<citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" count="1">16</citation>). <sentence_start/>The carrier frequency both in Irish patients and controls was high when compared to that reported in most European studies with the exception of Spain (9.8%, 22/225) (<citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.24045" pmid="22173904" count="1">31</citation>). <sentence_start/>The higher <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> frequency in Spain could be related to the higher rate of Jewish ancestry in the Iberian Peninsula (<citation rid="B32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neurobiolaging.2016.06.001" pmcid="PMC4976046" pmid="27393345" count="1">32</citation>).

While the number of p.N370S and RecNcil carriers was equal in Irish PD (with no carriers of p.L444P found), it has been reported that p.N370S is more prevalent in the Europeans and Ashkenazi Jews (70%), and p.L444P is the most common mutation in Chinese (62%) (<citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/01.wnl.0000304039.11891.29" pmid="18434642" count="1">27</citation>, <citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0115747" pmid="25535748" pmcid="PMC4275276" count="1">33</citation>). <sentence_start/>It could be argued that p.T369M should not be included in our pathogenic/risk group, as the number of p.T369M carriers was greater in the control group p.T369M (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 6) than in the PD group (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 5 heterozygotes and <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 1 compound heterozygote with p.E326K); however, we did include p.T369M variant in the pathogenic/risk group in agreement with the most recent literature (<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.27659" pmid="30957308" pmcid="PMC6579628" count="1">4</citation>, <citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.27845" pmid="31505070" pmcid="PMC7017876" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.27803" pmid="31769092" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/NXG.0000000000000104" pmid="27648471" pmcid="PMC5017539" count="1">15</citation>).

We detected a p.G377C (p.G416C, c.1246G > T) variant. <sentence_start/>The G > T nucleotide change in position 416 has not been found in the available databases; however, a change G > A (p.G416S, rs121908311) in the same position is classified as pathogenic. <sentence_start/>The β-glucosidase enzyme level in a heterozygote carrier within the normal range found in our patient is consistent with the report by Alcalay et al. (<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/brain/awv179" pmid="26117366" pmcid="PMC4564023" count="1">26</citation>) (p.E326K does not cause Gaucher's disease even in a homozygote state, and the enzymatic level is also within the normal range) (<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/brain/awv179" pmid="26117366" pmcid="PMC4564023" count="1">26</citation>). <sentence_start/>The p.G377C variant was described in one case study of Gaucher's disease from Northern Ireland (<citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" count="1">34</citation>) as a compound heterozygote, but not in PD. <sentence_start/>Only homozygous or compound heterozygous variants cause Gaucher's disease; therefore, p.G377C was necessary to contribute to the disease in the case report by Illingworth (<citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" count="1">34</citation>). <sentence_start/>Moreover, the level of plasma chitotriosidase was 8,000 in the Illingworth (<citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" count="1">34</citation>) case, further supporting symptomatic Gaucher's disease (the level of chitotriosidase is only elevated in symptomatic patients with Gaucher's disease). <sentence_start/>Taken together, these evidence support the likely pathogenicity of this variant.

We also identified a p.G195E variant implicated in Gaucher's disease (<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1172/JCI119437" pmid="9153297" pmcid="PMC508094" count="1">25</citation>) that cosegregated with PD, which merits further investigation (the at-risk siblings are now older than the affected, but we cannot exclude the development of PD at a later age due to the intrafamilial PD heterogeneity). <sentence_start/>This finding may suggest a more significant role of p.G195E in PD; however, this variant needs to be further explored.

There was no association of gender with pathogenic/risk variants in PD in keeping with findings from Lesage et al. where there was no difference detected (<citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddq454" pmid="20947659" count="1">9</citation>). <sentence_start/>Male/female ratio was also reported 5:1-3:2 in other studies (<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jmoldx.2017.05.005" pmid="28727984" count="1">35</citation>). <sentence_start/>Combined MCI-PD (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 5/26) and PDD (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 4/26) occurred in 34.6%. <sentence_start/>This is in keeping with other studies (24-48%) (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fneur.2016.00071" pmid="27242656" pmcid="PMC4861838" count="1">36</citation>). <sentence_start/>The more common cognitive decline (six-fold increased dementia risk) has been reported in the literature (<citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/NXG.0000000000000354" pmid="31404238" pmcid="PMC6659137" count="1">5</citation>, <citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.27845" pmid="31505070" pmcid="PMC7017876" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.24045" pmid="22173904" count="1">31</citation>), but the prevalence of cognitive impairment and dementia analyzed either separately or as one group in our study did not differ between carriers and non-carriers (however, the sample was small). <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> mutation/risk variant presence was independently associated with hallucinations in our study in keeping with other studies (<citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mds.24045" pmid="22173904" count="1">31</citation>). <sentence_start/>The three-fold higher occurrence of dyskinesia in the <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> carrier group in comparison to non-carriers in our study is in keeping with other reports. <sentence_start/>The higher occurrence of dyskinesia suggests that <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> carriers may be more sensitive to medications and genetic assessment in the appropriate patient should be taken into consideration (<citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1212/NXG.0000000000000354" pmid="31404238" pmcid="PMC6659137" count="1">5</citation>, <citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddq454" pmid="20947659" count="1">9</citation>, <citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fneur.2016.00071" pmid="27242656" pmcid="PMC4861838" count="1">36</citation>) (similarly to the levodopa sensitivity and more frequent dyskinesia resulting in small levodopa doses being used for parkin mutations carriers). <sentence_start/>While the number of patients with YOPD in the study (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 81) may seem high, and this group is interesting in itself from the genetic perspective, these were neither specifically preselected for the recruitment nor were they related in any way (only probands were reported in this study).

There are several strengths of our study including the examination of the <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> prevalence in Irish PD for the first time, the full sequencing of coding regions (and exon-intron boundaries) of the <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> gene on the 3.14% of the Irish PD population (314 PD patients recruited/10,000 number of PD patients in Ireland) (limited screening for p.N370S and p.L444P would result in 81.8% of the mutations being missed in our study), comparison to the ethnically matched control group with a high genotyping success rate, and comprehensive investigation of other causes of autosomal dominant and recessive PD (making this study the most comprehensive and up-to-date report of genetics of PD in the Irish population).

Our study also has a few limitations: it was an observational cross-sectional study; therefore, the progression of the disease could not be assessed, and a longitudinal study should be performed in the future. <sentence_start/>It should be noted that we were unable to reliably determine phase for the two individuals with a presumed compound heterozygous carrier state, both carried the risk variant E326K (E326K/T369M, <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 1; E326K/G377C, <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 1); however, these subjects would fall into the risk/pathogenic group regardless of being in “cis” or in “trans” status. <sentence_start/>While we acknowledge the small sample size of the control group in comparison to the PD group most likely leading to the non-significance of the <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> prevalence data, in our opinion, having a control group is an important part of any <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> study.

With the advent of new screening technologies, <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> carriers will be encountered more frequently in our clinics, and it will be essential to prepare a mutation-specific approach to the management of PD. <sentence_start/>Efforts to find a disease-modifying treatment for <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> carriers with PD are ongoing. <sentence_start/>There are currently two clinical trials underway, one trial examining ambroxol, an over-the-counter medication used to reduce mucus production in respiratory tract disorders, and its influence on motor and cognitive progression in <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> carriers, and a placebo controlled phase 2 double-blind study (MOVES-PD) of GZ/SAR4027671-a molecule capable of crossing brain-blood barrier (<citation rid="B37" ref-type="bibr" count="1">37</citation>, <citation rid="B38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12883-019-1252-3" pmid="30738426" pmcid="PMC6368728" count="1">38</citation>). <sentence_start/>Another recently completed trial showed that the target engagement and CSF penetration were accomplished in PD patients treated with oral ambroxol. <sentence_start/>While the CSF glucocerebrosidase activity decreased, the glucocerebrosidase protein levels and alpha-synuclein levels increased and UPDRS-III score improved by a mean of 6.8 points. <sentence_start/>Notably, these changes occurred both in patients with and without <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> mutations (<citation rid="B39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamaneurol.2019.4611" pmid="31930374" pmcid="PMC6990847" count="1">39</citation>). <sentence_start/>There are no recommendations of how to proceed, where the risk of PD is disclosed, but preventative approaches may be rapidly approaching. <sentence_start/>Patients should be informed about the increased possibility of cognitive decline, depression, falls, autonomic vulnerability, family (<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jmoldx.2017.05.005" pmid="28727984" count="1">35</citation>) planning, and disease progression [carriers are reported to die earlier at 75.7 years (SD 5.5) than non-carriers 80.9 (6.6)] (<citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/ene.13395" pmid="28834018" pmcid="PMC5657539" count="1">40</citation>). <sentence_start/>Treatment options for <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> mutation carriers should be a little bit distinct and focus on the avoidance of medications increasing the risk of falls (lowering blood pressure), worsening cognitive status, and deferral of levodopa therapy (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fneur.2016.00071" pmid="27242656" pmcid="PMC4861838" count="1">36</citation>). <sentence_start/>Further research is required, but personalized therapeutic approach for PD may be closer than we might think.
Conclusion

We present the most comprehensive and up-to-date overview of genetics of PD in the Irish population. <sentence_start/>We, for the first time, showed the link between <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> and PD in Ireland. <sentence_start/>In agreement with our hypothesis, the findings of our study suggest that the <italic toggle="yes">GBA</italic> prevalence in PD is higher than in most European countries, and genetic background of Irish PD patients warrants further studies.
